No body, no rig — the reconstruction itself

Skeleton On The Performer

The triangulated joints projected straight back through camera A001's own lens, drawn on the frame they came from. No mesh, no canonical rig, nothing that could flatter it — this is what the geometry actually produced, at each performer's own measured size.

frame 060
The dashed white figure is what we actually ship. Solid colour is the measured skeleton — the performer's own size. Dashed white is the delivered rig's joints, projected through the same lens. They separate by a median of 6.0 and 9.7 pixels, reaching 17–21 at p95, on figures only ~250 pixels tall. Watch the shoulders and the pelvis: the canonical rig is 540 mm across the shoulders against a measured 346–363 — roughly 185 mm too wide, so each arm starts about 90 mm further out than it should on both performers.

The two performers are not the same size — and the rig gives them the same body

This is the thing the render was telling you. Measured per performer, per take, by the pipeline itself:

segmentperformer Aperformer Bcanonical rig
pelvis → neck576.6513.3580
shoulder width346.4363.1540.0
upper arm287.2277.2260
forearm268.9258.0240
thigh399.8402.0430
shin396.5405.3420.5
hip width207.1214.5180

Their torsos differ by 63 mm and their shoulders by 17, and both are driven onto the same fixed skeleton — so both delivered characters are the same person wearing two performances.

But the largest error is not between the performers, it is the rig itself. Its shoulders are 540 mm apart where the performers measure 346 and 363. That single number puts each arm root about 90 mm too far out, and it is the best available explanation for the ~180 mm wrist displacement measured separately — the whole arm chain hangs from the wrong place before a single joint angle is applied. Every measurement here is on the same joint definition the landmarks use, which is what makes the comparison legitimate; an earlier version of this table compared the rig's clavicle joints instead and reported the error backwards.

The pipeline already measures every one of those numbers. estimate_limb_lengths_m computes them per subject per take — and the retarget then discards them and rebuilds on the canonical rest offsets. Putting them back recovers 19–35% of the proportion gap, and 39–63% on the legs.
What sizing will and will not fix. It will fix where the joints are — limbs stop disagreeing with the performer, the two characters stop being identical twins, hips stop floating. It will not make performer A look like performer A: girth, shoulders and mass distribution are dense shape, not skeleton, and that waits on a body scan. Sizing fixes proportions; the scan fixes the body. Nor does it touch the hands, which have no landmarks at all.
Read this overlay as a picture, not as a score. A skeleton that hugs the image is not evidence of 3D accuracy — error along the camera's own viewing ray is invisible in this projection, which is exactly why reprojection onto our own detections is banned as an acceptance gate in this project. It is here to show you what the geometry produced, not to argue that it is right.
Joints are the pipeline's retained triangulated_world_positions_z_up_m, projected through A001's published extrinsics and intrinsics scaled to 640×360. Frames are the pipeline's own extracted JPEGs. Every fifth frame of 150.
